citations.context: The Texas Deceptive Trade Practices–Consumer Protection Act ("DTPA"), Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 17.41–17.63, provides a cause of action for consumers who have been harmed by false, misleading, or deceptive acts or practices, unconscionable actions, or breaches of express or implied warranties.

first_check.quote_check: No quotations attributed.

citations.cited_for: nondisclosure as basis for fraud
citations.context: Haase v. Glazner, 62 S.W.3d 795 (Tex. 2001) (nondisclosure as basis for fraud)

first_check.quote_check: No quotations attributed.
first_check.explanation: The case and reporter cite are real and correct: Haase v. Glazner, 62 S.W.3d 795 (Tex. 2001). CourtListener lists a parallel cite of 2001 WL 1512608 and shows its 2002-01-17 date as the rehearing-overruled date, so the 2001 year is not a defect. The parenthetical is wrong. Haase does not address nondisclosure as a basis for fraud. It holds that (1) a fraudulent inducement claim cannot be asserted without a contract, and (2) the Statute of Frauds bars a fraud claim seeking benefit-of-the-bargain damages on an unenforceable contract, while out-of-pocket fraud damages may survive. first_check.quote_check: "more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully" - NOT found in Twombly (the word 'sheer' appears nowhere in the 550 U.S. 544 opinion, majority or dissent); found verbatim in Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678. "not akin to a 'probability requirement,' but it asks for more than a sheer possibility" - NOT found in Twombly; found verbatim in Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678.
first_check.explanation: Both quotations attributed to Twombly at 556 are actually Iqbal's later paraphrase of Twombly, at 556 U.S. 678. Twombly at 556 says only that asking for plausible grounds 'does not impose a probability requirement at the pleading stage'; it does not use the 'not akin to' or 'sheer possibility' language. The underlying proposition is sound law and Twombly 556 supports the 'no probability requirement' half, but the quoted words belong to Iqbal and should be cited there. (The memo itself, in its Iqbal section, elsewhere attributes the 'not akin to a probability requirement' language to Iqbal at 678.)
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556: "Asking for plausible grounds to infer an agreement does not impose a probability requirement at the pleading stage; it simply calls for enough fact to raise a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of illegal agreement." Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678: "The plausibility standard is not akin to a "probability requirement," but it asks for more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully. Ibid."

second_check.explanation: Finding holds. Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556, reads: 'Asking for plausible grounds to infer an agreement does not impose a probability requirement at the pleading stage; it simply calls for enough fact to raise a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of illegal agreement.' A literal search of the full Twombly opinion for 'sheer possibility' returned 0 matches, and the opinion has no 'not akin to' language. The quoted sentence is Iqbal's: 'The plausibility standard is not akin to a "probability requirement," but it asks for more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully. Ibid.' (556 U.S. at 678, citing Twombly at 556). The proposition is sound law, and Twombly 556 supports the no-probability-requirement half. But the quoted words do not appear in the authority cited ('Id.' = Twombly), so MISQUOTED is correct. The correct cite is Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678 (citing Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556).

first_check.quote_check: (1) "not akin to a probability requirement" - found at 678 with a minor difference (original: not akin to a "probability requirement," with internal quotation marks). (2) "calls for enough fact to raise a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence" - NOT FOUND anywhere in Iqbal (full-text search of the U.S. Reports text); it is Twombly's own language at 550 U.S. at 556, and Iqbal does not quote it. (3) "Where a complaint pleads facts that are 'merely consistent with' a defendant's liability, it 'stops short of the line between possibility and plausibility of entitlement to relief.'" - found at 678, essentially verbatim (original has inner quotation marks around 'entitlement to relief'). second_check.explanation: Partially refuted: the defect is real, but calling it MISQUOTED overstates it. Three of the four quotes are verbatim in Iqbal at the cited pages. At 678: 'The plausibility standard is not akin to a "probability requirement," ...' and 'Where a complaint pleads facts that are "merely consistent with" a defendant's liability, it "stops short of the line between possibility and plausibility of 'entitlement to relief.'"' At 679: 'be a context-specific task that requires the reviewing court to draw on its judicial experience and common sense.' The fourth quote, 'calls for enough fact to raise a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence', is not in Iqbal (search returned 0 matches). The error is citation form: Iqbal did not reproduce that phrase, so it should be cited directly to Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556. The memo also drops the inner quotation marks around 'probability requirement'. The propositions are correct law, and every quoted word exists in the named sources, so this is better classed as a minor attribution defect than as misquotation.

citations.cited_for: DTPA exemption for transactions involving total consideration over $500,000 unless consumer is an individual; dispositive of Count V
citations.context: Section 17.49(f) of the DTPA provides an exemption from DTPA claims for transactions involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, unless the consumer is an individual. Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.49(f).

first_check.correct_citation: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.49(g)
first_check.quote_check: No quotations attributed.
first_check.explanation: The memo's 'Statutory Text' paragraph says § 17.49(f) exempts transactions with total consideration over $500,000 'unless the consumer is an individual'. That is wrong on two points. First, the $500,000 exemption is subsection (g); subsection (f) is a different exemption for written contracts over $100,000 where the consumer had independent legal counsel and no residence is involved. Second, neither subsection has an 'individual consumer' exception: the only carve-out in (g) is for 'a cause of action involving a consumer's residence', so an individual in a non-residential transaction over $500,000 is also exempt. The conclusion that Arcadia's $17,050,000 transaction is exempt is still supported by § 17.49(g).
first_check.evidence_excerpt: (g) Nothing in this subchapter shall apply to a cause of action arising from a transaction, a project, or a set of transactions relating to the same project, involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. I read the current Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.49 on the Texas Legislature site. Subsection (f) covers "a claim arising out of a written contract if: (1) ... total consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000; (2) ... the consumer is represented by legal counsel ...; and (3) the contract does not involve the consumer's residence." The $500,000 exemption is in (g): "involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence." Neither subsection carves out individual consumers. The only carve-out is for the consumer's residence. So the memo gives the wrong subsection and invents an 'individual' exception. Its conclusion that a $17.05M non-residential deal is exempt is still supported by (g), and might be by (f) if Arcadia had independent counsel. The cite error alone might support WRONG_CITATION_REAL_CASE, but the misstated statutory content makes MISCHARACTERIZED the better status.

citations.authority: Brasby and Kuhn (economic loss doctrine); Sharyland and Chapman (Texas economic loss rule)
citations.cited_for: Delaware economic loss doctrine as articulated in Brasby and Kuhn; economic loss rule as applied in Sharyland and Chapman
citations.context: Delaware's economic loss doctrine, as articulated in Brasby and Kuhn, provides additional protection against attempts to recharacterize contract claims as tort claims.

first_check.correct_citation: Kuhn Construction, Inc. v. Diamond State Port Corp., 990 A.2d 393 (Del. 2010) (arbitration case, not economic loss); Sharyland Water Supply Corp. v. City of Alton, 354 S.W.3d 407 (Tex. 2011); Chapman Custom Homes, Inc. v. Dallas Plumbing Co., 445 S.W.3d 716 (Tex. 2014); only real "Brasby" located: Brasby v. Morris, 2007 WL 949485 (Del. Super. Ct. Mar. 29, 2007)
first_check.quote_check: No quotation attributed in this short-form reference.
first_check.explanation: Four short-form authorities. (1) Brasby: no Delaware Supreme Court case "Brasby v. Morris Dynamics, Inc., 947 A.2d 1042" exists (see refs 73/153); the only real namesake is an unpublished Superior Court decision, Brasby v. Morris. (2) Kuhn, 990 A.2d 393, is real but is a referee/arbitration-clause case: the Delaware Supreme Court reversed an order compelling arbitration; the opinion contains zero occurrences of "economic loss" or "tort." It does not articulate Delaware's economic loss doctrine at all. (3) Sharyland and (4) Chapman are real Texas Supreme Court cases that do state the general Texas economic loss rule, but both HELD the rule did not bar the negligence claims before them (Sharyland reversed the court of appeals on that point; Chapman: "the rule does not apply here"). So "Delaware's economic loss doctrine, as articulated in Brasby and Kuhn" is unsupported for both Delaware authorities, and the Texas cases support only the general statement of the rule, not its application to bar claims.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Kuhn: "Because the referee clause on these facts do not clearly require arbitration and Kuhn may litigate its claims, we reverse the judgment of the Court of Chancery." Sharyland: "Because we conclude that the economic loss rule does not preclude a negligence claim against the contractors ..." Chapman: "The economic loss rule generally precludes recovery in tort for economic losses resulting from a party's failure to perform under a contract when the harm consists only of the economic loss of a contractual expectancy. ... But it does not bar all tort claims arising out of a contractual setting."

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. Kuhn, 990 A.2d 393, is an arbitration and referee-clause case, and the opinion has zero occurrences of "economic loss" or "misrepresent". It articulates no economic loss doctrine. One partial mitigation for Brasby: the real unpublished decision Brasby v. Morris, 2007 WL 949485 (Del. Super. Ct. Mar. 29, 2007), does state Delaware's economic loss doctrine. CB Lewes v. Brightfields (Del. Super. 2020) quotes it: "[t]here exists no reason to extend tort law into areas that can be adequately governed by contract law." So the short-form "Brasby" proposition has some real support, but the memo's version (Del. Supreme Court, 947 A.2d 1042, defendant "Morris Dynamics") does not exist. Because the Kuhn half is wholly unsupported, the sentence remains mischaracterized. Sharyland and Chapman state the general Texas rule, as the first reviewer noted.

citations.authority: Twombly / Iqbal / Lormand; Fortune Production; Excess Underwriters; Sloane; Benchmark; Rule 9(b); § 17.49(f)
citations.citation_as_written: Twombly/Iqbal; Lormand; Fortune Production; Excess Underwriters; Sloane; Benchmark; Section 17.49(f); Rule 9(b)
citations.cited_for: Recommended use of authorities in brief outline: Legal Standard (Twombly/Iqbal, Lormand), Count V (§ 17.49(f)), Count IV (Fortune Production, Excess Underwriters controlling), Count III (Sloane; Benchmark for 9(b))
citations.context: Legal Standard — Twombly/Iqbal and Fifth Circuit applications (Lormand). ... Fortune Production and Excess Underwriters are controlling.

first_check.correct_citation: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.49(g) (the more-than-$500,000 total-consideration exemption; carve-out is for a consumer's residence, not for individuals)
first_check.quote_check: No quotes attributed.
first_check.explanation: Compound entry; seven of the eight components check out and one does not. SUPPORTED: Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, and Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, are the pleading standard. Lormand, 565 F.3d 228 (5th Cir. 2009), applies Twombly's plausibility standard and says courts consider documents incorporated into the complaint by reference (note: Lormand was filed Apr. 9, 2009, before Iqbal on May 18, 2009, so it is a Twombly application only, and it does not use the memo's 'central to the plaintiff's claim' wording). Fortune Production, 52 S.W.3d 671 (Tex. 2000), holds unjust enrichment is unavailable where a valid express contract covers the subject matter. Excess Underwriters, 246 S.W.3d 42 (Tex. 2008), follows Fortune on that point, though as an additional reason in an insurer-reimbursement case rather than as its main holding. Sloane, 825 S.W.2d 439, limits negligent-misrepresentation damages to pecuniary reliance loss and excludes benefit-of-the-bargain damages. Benchmark, 343 F.3d 719 (5th Cir. 2003), applies Rule 9(b) to negligent-misrepresentation claims resting on the same facts as fraud claims (though it held those pleadings sufficient). Rule 9(b) is as described. NOT SUPPORTED: the outline's lead argument cites § 17.49(f) as a dispositive, purely legal exemption turning on $17,050,000 total consideration and Arcadia being an LLC (the memo elsewhere describes (f) as a more-than-$500,000 exemption 'unless the consumer is an individual'). That is not what (f) says. Subsection (f) covers claims arising out of a written contract involving more than $100,000 where the consumer was represented by independent legal counsel and no residence is involved. The more-than-$500,000 total-consideration exemption is subsection (g), and its only carve-out is for a consumer's residence; neither subsection turns on entity status. Caveat on severity: the conclusion that the DTPA claim is exempt is still supportable under (g), and plausibly under (f) on the counsel-representation facts, so this is a wrong subsection plus a misstated statutory condition rather than a wrong result. A reviewer could reasonably grade this as a minor defect on that basis.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Statute as quoted by the Houston First Court of Appeals: "Section 17.49(g) exempts from the DTPA 'a cause of action arising from a transaction, a project, or a set of transactions relating to the same project, involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000 . . . .'" and "other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence." Subsection (f) per texas.public.law: "(1) the contract relates to a transaction ... involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000; (2) in negotiating the contract the consumer is represented by legal counsel ...; and (3) the contract does not involve the consumer's residence." Excess Underwriters: "[w]hen a valid agreement already addresses the matter, recovery under an equitable theory is generally inconsistent with the express agreement."

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The case components (Twombly, Iqbal, Lormand, Fortune Production, Excess Underwriters, Sloane, Benchmark) are real. The defect is the statutory lead argument. The memo says § 17.49(f) exempts transactions over $500,000 'unless the consumer is an individual'. The statute does not say that. Subsection (f) reads: 'Nothing in the subchapter shall apply to a claim arising out of a written contract if: (1) ... total consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000; (2) ... the consumer is represented by legal counsel ...; and (3) the contract does not involve the consumer's residence.' The $500,000 exemption is subsection (g): '... involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence.' Neither subsection turns on whether the consumer is an individual. The exemption conclusion is likely still reachable under (g), so this is a wrong subsection plus an invented statutory condition, not a wrong result. That is why this is a borderline MISCHARACTERIZED rather than fabricated.

first_check.correct_citation: McCamish, Martin, Brown & Loeffler v. F.E. Appling Interests, 991 S.W.2d 787, 791-92 (Tex. 1999). The four-element formulation the memo puts in quotation marks is from Federal Land Bank Ass'n of Tyler v. Sloane, 825 S.W.2d 439, 442 (Tex. 1991).
first_check.quote_check: No quote was listed for this ref, but the memo puts a four-element formulation in quotation marks and cites it to McCamish at 791 ("(1) the representation is made by a defendant in the course of his business ... (4) the plaintiff suffers pecuniary loss by justifiably relying on the representation"). Not found in McCamish. Found verbatim in Sloane, 825 S.W.2d at 442, which McCamish cites at 791. McCamish at 791 instead block-quotes Restatement (Second) of Torts § 552(1), which covers the same elements in different words.
first_check.explanation: The case exists and the reporter cite is correct. The first proposition (elements of negligent misrepresentation under Restatement § 552) is supported in substance at 791, though the quoted wording belongs to Sloane. The second proposition is not what the case holds. McCamish held that a nonclient may sue an attorney for negligent misrepresentation without privity. The "independent duty" language at 792 explains why privity is not required, which widens liability. The court did not limit liability to cases where the defendant owes a duty "independent of any contractual obligations," and it did not require a contracting party to identify a duty outside the contract. The limits the court actually discussed are the § 552(2) limited class of claimants and justifiable reliance (793-94). The memo's conclusion that "under McCamish, Arcadia must identify a duty independent of the MSLSA" has no basis in the opinion. This is a judgment call: there is a textual hook at 792, so a lenient reader could treat it as a loose paraphrase.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Under the tort of negligent misrepresentation, liability is not based on the breach of duty a professional owes his or her clients or others in privity, but on an independent duty to the non-client based on the professional's manifest awareness of the nonclient's reliance on the misrepresentation and the professional's intention that the nonclient so rely. ... we conclude that there is no reason to exempt lawyers from the operation of section 552 or to impose a privity requirement on a negligent misrepresentation cause of action under section 552.

second_check.explanation: McCamish, 991 S.W.2d 787 (Tex. 1999), is real (CourtListener 1533840). It quotes Restatement § 552(1) verbatim ("One who, in the course of his business, profession or employment, or in any transaction in which he has a pecuniary interest, supplies false information..."), but the memo's numbered four-element quotation does not appear in the opinion: a search for "false information" finds only the § 552 block quote. The only "independent" passage is: "liability is not based on the breach of duty a professional owes his or her clients or others in privity, but on an independent duty to the non-client based on the professional's manifest awareness of the nonclient's reliance". That passage expands liability to nonclients who lack privity. It does not limit negligent misrepresentation to duties independent of a contract between the parties. The only other uses of "contract" describe plaintiffs "who are not parties to a contract for professional services" recovering. The memo's limiting rule is not what the case holds, so the finding stands. There is a textual hook at 792, which makes this a judgment call, but the characterization runs in the opposite direction from the opinion.

(2) "Available only where the defendant owes an independent duty and damages are out-of-pocket. (3) "Where the true complaint is non-delivery of what was contractually promised, the claim sounds in contract, not tort. Id. at 443": no such statement. Page 443 denies mental anguish damages and lost profits because the Sloanes "should not ... receive the benefit of a bargain that would never have taken place." Under the legal theory of this section of the Restatement, they should not, therefore, receive the benefit of a bargain that would never have taken place." ... second_check.explanation: I read the full opinion: Federal Land Bank Ass'n of Tyler v. Sloane, 825 S.W.2d 439, decided 1991-12-04, so the memo's year of 1992 is also off. The court did not bar the claim. It affirmed liability: 'The bank makes no challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence of liability, so the remaining issue is what damages are available for this tort.' It then remanded 'for rendition of judgment for $11,427.03 for past pecuniary losses other than lost profits.' The opinion never uses the phrases 'independent duty' or 'out-of-pocket', and never says benefit-of-the-bargain losses are 'recoverable only in contract'. first_check.quote_check: No quotations attributed.
first_check.explanation: Section 17.49 exists, but subsection (f) is not the rule the memo relies on. Subsection (f) is a three-part written-contract exemption: consideration over $100,000, the consumer represented in negotiation by independent legal counsel, and no consumer's residence involved. The memo's 'transaction-value exemption' (defined in its Section V.C as over $500,000, 'unless the consumer is an individual', and said to require no factual disputes) is subsection (g), which exempts transactions over $500,000 'other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence'. No part of § 17.49 contains an 'individual consumer' exception. The memo's conclusion (a $17,050,000 non-residential commercial transaction is exempt) does hold under § 17.49(g), but the cited subsection and the stated rule are wrong. CourtListener does not carry statute text, so the official Texas Legislature text was read.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: (f) Nothing in the subchapter shall apply to a claim arising out of a written contract if: (1) the contract relates to a transaction, a project, or a set of transactions related to the same project involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000; ... (g) Nothing in this subchapter shall apply to a cause of action arising from a transaction, a project, or a set of transactions relating to the same project, involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence.

second_check.explanation: I read the official Texas text. § 17.49(f) covers 'a claim arising out of a written contract' if '(1) ... total consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000; (2) in negotiating the contract the consumer is represented by legal counsel who is not directly or indirectly identified, suggested, or selected by the defendant ...; and (3) the contract does not involve the consumer's residence.' The memo's 'transaction-value exemption' (over $500,000, 'unless the consumer is an individual', no factual disputes) is really § 17.49(g): 'total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence.' Neither subsection has an exception for individual consumers. One nuance: the memo says Arcadia was represented by outside counsel, so § 17.49(f) could arguably apply on its own terms. But that would turn on the fact question of whether the counsel was independent of the defendant, which contradicts the memo's 'no factual disputes' claim, and the memo states the wrong rule for (f) anyway. The finding stands: right conclusion, but under § 17.49(g), not (f).

The $25 million figure comes from § 17.45(4), which excludes from the definition of 'consumer' 'a business consumer that has assets of $25 million or more, or that is owned or controlled by a corporation or entity with assets of $25 million or more.' Note: the $500,000 exemption the task documents label § 17.49(f) is actually § 17.49(g).
first_check.quote_check: "producing cause": found verbatim in Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.50(a).
first_check.explanation: All three additional DTPA dismissal grounds named in the rubric are real Texas law. Producing cause is a statutory element in § 17.50(a). Duplication of a contract claim is supported by Crawford, which holds that a mere breach of contract, without more, is not a DTPA violation. Separately, the rubric's "§ 17.49(f)" label for the $500,000 exemption is off: subsection (f) is the $100,000 written-contract exemption for a consumer represented by counsel, and the $500,000 exemption is subsection (g). Crawford: "An allegation of a mere breach of contract, without more, does not constitute a 'false, misleading or deceptive act' in violation of the DTPA." § 17.50(a): "A consumer may maintain an action where any of the following constitute a producing cause of economic damages or damages for mental anguish"

City of Alton, 354 S.W.3d 407, 415-18 (Tex. 2011), confirms that parties may be barred from recovering in negligence or strict liability for purely economic losses, and that Texas has applied the rule to defective products and failure to perform a contract. citations.authority: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) and 12(c)
citations.citation_as_written: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6); Rule 12(c)
citations.cited_for: Post-answer 12(b)(6) motion treated as a motion to dismiss, not a 12(c) motion, if conditions met
citations.context: a party that has filed an Answer may file a motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) — and the Court shall treat such motion as a motion to dismiss, not as a motion for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c)

first_check.correct_citation: Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b), 12(c), 12(h)(2)(B); see Jones v. Greninger, 188 F.3d 322, 324 (5th Cir. 1999) (post-answer 12(b)(6) motion is untimely and is treated as a Rule 12(c) motion)
first_check.quote_check: No quotation attributed to the rule.
first_check.explanation: Both rules exist, but the standing order's stated practice contradicts them. Rule 12(b) requires a 12(b)(6) motion to be made before pleading, and Rule 12(h)(2)(B) routes a later failure-to-state-a-claim challenge through a Rule 12(c) motion. The Fifth Circuit in Jones v. Greninger held a post-answer 12(b)(6) motion untimely and properly construed as a 12(c) motion. The standing order says the opposite: such a motion will be treated as a motion to dismiss, 'not' as a 12(c) motion. In fairness, this is a labeling conflict more than a substantive one, since the two motions are judged by the same standard (Doe v. MySpace, 528 F.3d 413, 418 (5th Cir. 2008)), and the provision is framed as the judge's own practice, so VERIFIED_MINOR_DEFECT is a defensible alternative reading. Two internal conflicts are worth flagging to a drafter: the standing order disclaims any power to 'modify or supersede the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure', and the scheduling order in the same case says the Court 'will treat any such motion as a Rule 12(c) motion' (ref 297).
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Rule 12(b): "A motion asserting any of these defenses must be made before pleading if a responsive pleading is allowed." Jones v. Greninger: "Because a rule 12(b) motion must be filed before responsive pleadings, the appellees' motion was untimely. Rule 12(c) motions, however, may be filed after the pleadings are closed. Such motions will be treated as a motion for judgment on the pleadings based on a failure to state a claim on which relief may be granted."

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. Rule 12(b) (LII): "A motion asserting any of these defenses must be made before pleading if a responsive pleading is allowed." Rule 12(h)(2): failure to state a claim may be raised "(B) by a motion under Rule 12(c)." Jones v. Greninger, 188 F.3d 322 (5th Cir. 1999): "Because a rule 12(b) motion must be filed before responsive pleadings, the appellees' motion was untimely. ... Such motions will be treated as a motion for judgment on the pleadings." The standing order says the opposite: it will treat a post-answer 12(b)(6) motion 'as a motion to dismiss, not as a motion for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c).' The scenario's own Scheduling Order also contradicts it ('The Court will treat any such motion as a Rule 12(c) motion'). The two motions are judged by the same standard, so the practical effect is mostly about labeling. Even so, the stated practice conflicts with the text of the cited rules and with binding Fifth Circuit authority.

Under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c)(1), a corporation is 'deemed to be a citizen of every State ... by which it has been incorporated and of the State ... where it has its principal place of business.' That makes both parties Texas citizens, so the case is not between 'citizens of different States' under § 1332(a)(1). Para. 15's reasoning, that diversity exists because Meridian's Delaware citizenship is not shared, does not follow from that text. Separately, § 1441(b)(2) says a diversity-only action 'may not be removed if any of the parties in interest properly joined and served as defendants is a citizen of the State in which such action is brought.' The statutes are correctly identified, but on the facts the Notice recites they do not make removal proper. The statement in para. 25 is therefore unsupported by the cited authority.

second_check.explanation: I could not refute this finding. I read the official Texas statute text (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 17). Section 17.49(f) reads: "Nothing in the subchapter shall apply to a claim arising out of a written contract if: (1) the contract relates to a transaction ... involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $100,000; (2) in negotiating the contract the consumer is represented by legal counsel ...; and (3) the contract does not involve the consumer's residence." It has no $500,000 figure and no $25 million asset prong. The $500,000 exemption is § 17.49(g): "Nothing in this subchapter shall apply to a cause of action arising from a transaction ... involving total consideration by the consumer of more than $500,000, other than a cause of action involving a consumer's residence." That exemption has no asset condition. The $25 million language appears only in the § 17.45(4) definition of "consumer": "the term does not include a business consumer that has assets of $25 million or more." So the letter's "conjunctive" reading, which requires both $500,000 in consideration and $25 million in assets, is not in § 17.49(f) or anywhere else in the statute. On the letter's own concession that consideration exceeded $500,000, § 17.49(g) would apply regardless of Arcadia's assets. The phrase "total assets" appears 0 times in the subchapter, so the claim that it is a "defined accounting concept" under § 17.49(f) has no textual basis. The quoted statutory language attributed to (f) is a garbled blend of (g) and § 17.45(4). Because the statute is cited for a rule it does not contain, MISCHARACTERIZED is the right status.
